summary:
PYRO 07 is an AI-powered research platform designed to make NASA's microgravity combustion data accessible, understandable, and actionable for future spacecraft fire safety.

Developed for NASA Space Apps' Flame in Freefall challenge, our platform integrates 512 NASA experiments and 7,393 measurements from BASS-II, FLEX, and SAME-R, covering flame behavior, fire extinction, and smoke detection.

PYRO 07 combines hybrid semantic search, interactive scientific comparisons, an evidence relationship map, and a live Claude-powered research assistant. Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the assistant retrieves authentic NASA evidence, generates explanations with verified citations, and clearly identifies scientific uncertainties.

Alongside the deployed platform, we developed an experimental 3D fire-forecasting concept featuring a configurable 10×10 environment, gravity and airflow controls, smoke detector placement, and scenario comparisons. Its simulations are illustrative and not yet validated against NASA experimental data.

Our vision is to bridge the gap between complex space research and practical safety decisions—helping researchers and engineers explore evidence, investigate fire risks, and develop better-informed approaches to protecting future space missions.

PYRO 07 — AI-Powered Microgravity Fire Research

THE PROBLEM

Fire is one of the most serious hazards in crewed space exploration. Under microgravity, the absence of normal buoyancy-driven convection changes how flames develop, how liquid and solid fuels burn, and how smoke moves through enclosed environments. This creates challenges for fire prevention, detection, and suppression aboard spacecraft and future lunar or Martian habitats.

NASA has conducted extensive combustion research aboard the International Space Station. However, understanding the relationships between experimental conditions, measurements, scientific findings, and source documentation requires navigating multiple datasets and technical resources.

OUR SOLUTION

PYRO 07 is a publicly accessible research platform that brings authentic NASA microgravity combustion evidence into one interactive environment.

The deployed platform contains 512 experimental records and 7,393 published measurements, organized around three NASA investigations:

BASS-II — Burning and Suppression of Solids II: 129 indexed experiments exploring solid-fuel combustion and flammability under microgravity conditions.

FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment: 274 indexed experiments investigating liquid-fuel droplet combustion and flame extinction.

SAME-R — Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Reflight: 109 indexed records related to smoke and aerosol measurements relevant to spacecraft fire detection.

The platform also contains 1,368 indexed evidence passages and preserves the provenance of 19 verified NASA source files.

HOW THE PLATFORM WORKS

1. NASA Evidence Integration

Original NASA files are processed into a structured SQLite database. Published measurements, experimental identifiers, units, supporting documents, and source references are preserved. File integrity is checked using SHA-256 hashes.

2. Hybrid Evidence Search

Our search engine combines keyword-based retrieval with semantic similarity using locally executed sentence-transformer embeddings. This allows users to find relevant NASA experiments and scientific passages using natural-language questions.

3. Ask PYRO — Evidence-Grounded AI

Our live AI research assistant uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). It retrieves relevant NASA evidence, passes that context to Anthropic Claude, and presents an explanation with traceable citations.

Rather than treating an AI-generated answer as automatically correct, the backend validates source references and checks whether the generated claims are supported by retrieved material. Supported findings are distinguished from AI interpretation. When evidence is insufficient, PYRO 07 explicitly reports uncertainty or declines to make an unsupported conclusion.

4. Scientific Experiment Exploration

Users can examine individual experimental records, review published measurements and original values, inspect scientific conditions, and verify supporting NASA sources.

5. Interactive Scientific Comparison

PYRO 07 generates visual comparisons from compatible experimental measurements. Charts distinguish observed NASA values from statistics calculated by the application. Measurements with unresolved units or incompatible definitions are not silently treated as comparable.

6. Evidence Map

An interactive relationship graph connects investigations, experiments, source documents, and scientific concepts. The graph distinguishes source-supported relationships from derived or inferred connections, helping users understand the structure and provenance of the evidence.

EXPERIMENTAL FORECASTING CONCEPT

In parallel with the main application, our team explored a separate 3D fire-forecasting concept for future research.

The prototype allows users to configure a 10×10 environment, change gravity and airflow conditions, explore hypothetical fire spread, position smoke detectors, compare scenarios, and examine possible responses through interactive 3D visualizations.

This is an illustrative, heuristic simulation rather than a validated fire-prediction model. Its numerical outcomes have not been calibrated against BASS-II, FLEX, or SAME-R measurements. It is not integrated into the deployed PYRO 07 research platform and must not be used for real-world safety decisions.

The concept demonstrates a possible future direction: connecting explainable scenario exploration with experimentally validated scientific models.

TECHNOLOGIES USED

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and React Flow.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, and Pydantic.

Database: SQLite with full-text search and structured experimental measurements.

Semantic retrieval: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence-transformer embeddings executed locally using ONNX.

Generative AI: Anthropic Claude through a retrieval-augmented research workflow.

Deployment: Docker and Railway cloud hosting.

Experimental 3D concept: Babylon.js and browser-based simulation logic.

DEVELOPMENT AND DESIGN

The application was developed through an iterative engineering process with automated backend and frontend testing, browser interaction checks, accessibility testing, and verification against real NASA data.

The interface emphasizes readable scientific information, source traceability, responsive layouts, and transparent communication of data limitations.

WHY IT MATTERS

PYRO 07 addresses an important gap between scientific data availability and scientific accessibility.

By combining authentic experimental records, hybrid search, interactive visualizations, and citation-grounded AI, the platform helps researchers, engineers, students, and space enthusiasts investigate combustion evidence without losing the connection to its original sources.

Our longer-term vision is to support the development of experimentally grounded forecasting and decision-support tools for future space missions.

SCIENTIFIC RESPONSIBILITY

PYRO 07 is a research-support prototype, not a certified spacecraft fire-safety system. The current indexed datasets do not establish every outcome needed for predictive fire-risk modeling. In particular, the available BASS-II tables do not provide measured flame-spread labels, and the indexed SAME-R tables do not provide complete smoke-outcome labels.

We therefore distinguish published observations, application-computed comparisons, AI-generated explanations, and illustrative forecasting concepts.

Our objective is not to replace scientific judgment, but to make NASA's evidence more discoverable, understandable, and useful as a foundation for future research.

EXPERIMENTAL 3D FIRE FORECAST LAB

Alongside the main PYRO 07 research platform, our team developed an interactive 3D fire-forecasting concept to explore future spacecraft fire-safety applications.

The prototype allows users to simulate illustrative fire-spread scenarios across a configurable 10×10 environment, adjust gravity, oxygen and airflow conditions, position smoke detectors, compare scenarios, and explore hypothetical safety responses.

This experimental simulation uses heuristic models and has not been scientifically calibrated or validated against NASA combustion datasets. It is presented as a proof of concept for future research, not as a reliable fire-risk prediction or operational safety tool.
